query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount of molybdenum (approximately 0.2 at.%) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will modify the phase balance in its fine lamellar microstructure to improve both its strength and ductility, thereby enhancing its resistance to room-temperature creep, long-term mechanical loading, and corrosive degradation in service as fasteners.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in the as-cast condition (with coupled fcc and B2 phases).
generation.intervention: Add 0.2 at.% Mo during alloy fabrication to obtain a Mo-doped AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be processed under the same eutectic casting conditions as the baseline, and its performance will be evaluated under service-relevant tests including tensile tests (at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to approximately 700°C), long-term creep tests at room temperature, cyclic thermal fluctuation tests, and corrosion testing in environments simulating industrial corrosive conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The Mo addition is expected to slightly alter the relative volumes and distribution of the soft fcc (L12) and hard B2 phases and may refine the lamellar spacing, thereby enhancing dislocation interactions and promoting a more beneficial composite behavior.
generation.mechanism: Molybdenum acts as a solid solution strengthener and modifies the lamellar phase ratio, leading to improved load transfer between the ductile and strong phases. This adjustment reinforces the overall resistance to deformation under long-term loading and creep while also potentially improving corrosion resistance by stabilizing the phase structure under extreme conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting alloy, the Mo-doped alloy is expected to show an increase in tensile strength (on the order of several percent up to roughly 34% improvement based on prior observations) and an enhancement in fracture elongation (maintaining or exceeding a 24% elongation), resulting in better overall mechanical performance and durability under cyclic thermal and corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: The original as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure exhibiting strength and plasticity below industrial requirements.
generation.boundary: Operating conditions include room temperature up to approximately 700°C, exposure to cyclical thermal fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading (including creep conditions at room temperature), and corrosive environments typical of industrial fastener applications.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Mo content and the precise balance between phase volume fractions may vary slightly depending on processing nuances; while literature indicates performance improvements with ~0.2 at.% Mo, quantitative gains under all service conditions remain to be fully verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and (b) the Mo-doped AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy with 0.2 at.% Mo added during alloying. Ensure both sets undergo identical casting and thermo-mechanical processing. Subject samples to standardized tensile tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to ~700°C), long-term room-temperature creep tests, cyclic thermal shock tests, and corrosion resistance evaluation in a simulated industrial corrosive medium.
measurements: Room-temperature and elevated-temperature tensile strength and fracture elongation
Creep strain rate under constant load at room temperature
Thermal cycling durability (number of cycles until performance degradation)
Corrosion rate (mass loss or electrochemical measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement (beyond experimental error margins) in tensile strength, ductility, creep resistance, and corrosion performance compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis that the 0.2 at.% Mo addition enhances performance for fastener applications will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4a shows the stress–strain curves and corresponding fracture morphologies of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1Xy (X = V, Mo, B; y = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3) EHEAs. The tensile strength of the alloys increases and then decreases with the increase in the high-melting-point metals V and Mo, which results from the change in the ratio of the FCC phase to the BCC phase in these alloys. The mechanical properties of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1Xy alloy are more affected by changes in the B contents compared with the V and Mo. The tensile strength of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1By alloy decreases significantly with increasing B elements, and the best mechanical properties were found in the B0.1 alloy. The tensile property of the Mo0.2 alloy is superior to that of the other two alloys with different contents. The tensile strength of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy is greatly increased after adding 0.2 at.% Mo, while the alloy still retains a fracture elongation of more than 24%, as listed in Table 2. The Mo0.2 alloy presents the maximum strength and plasticity when compared to other types of eutectic high-entropy alloy. Its tensile strength is enhanced by 3.6~34%, and its fracture elongation is raised by 0.9~2.9 times.
